blocks.text: The coronary circulation or myocardial circulation is the nourishing circulation of the heart itself. The term “coronary” alludes to the morphological appearance of the initial arteries which form a crown around the heart. As an organ circulation, it is connected directly to the arterial system.

The large coronary arteries, which arise from the root of the aorta, are located on the surface of the heart and the small arteries plunge from the surface into the muscular mass; it is through these arteries that the heart receives virtually all of its supply.
The left coronary mainly supplies the anterior and lateral walls of the left ventricle (LV)
The right coronary irrigates the right ventricle (RV) and the posterior wall of the heart.
Most of the coronary venous return from the LV occurs through the coronary sinus which receives approximately 75% of the total coronary circulation.

Most of the blood that irrigates the RV returns directly to the right atrium (RA) via small anterior cardiac veins. A small amount of coronary flow returns to the left heart via the tiny veins of Thebesius which open directly into the heart chambers.

The coronary arteries are arteries that twist to accommodate the contractions of the heart. They are of the terminal type: the total obstruction of a branch therefore leads to the cessation of circulation in this region (myocardial infarction).
Coronary circulation is dominated by two facts:

-it is located, for its functional part, in an organ which contracts rhythmically and therefore creates a tension, which, at the level of the LV, reaches a value such that the vessels, even arterial ones, are crushed; it follows that irrigation is blocked during a notable part of the contraction;
-the myocardium, always active, has a high metabolism; it also requires a significant supply of nutrients and even more oxygen.
The pressure at entry into the coronary arterial system is that which prevails in the aorta.

But the contraction of the myocardium creates a high tissue pressure, higher than the arterial blood pressure, which has the effect of crushing the intra-parietal vessels and consequently interrupting blood flow; this however at the level of the LV where the pressure reaches high values.

The average coronary flow is approximately 0.8 ml/min/g of myocardium for the left ventricle and 0.6 ml/min/g of myocardium for the right ventricle, but this average value is subject to great variability in time and space and can be multiplied by 4 or 5 during exercise.
Instantaneous coronary flow is subject to variations in intramyocardial pressure.
In the LV wall in particular, during the isovolumetric contraction phase, intramyocardial pressure is high and coronary flow is low.
Instantaneous coronary flow is subject to variations in intramyocardial pressure.
In the LV wall in particular, during the isovolumetric contraction phase, intramyocardial pressure is high and coronary flow is low.

It increases at the start of the ventricular ejection phase due to the rapid decrease in ventricular volume which leads to a drop in intramyocardial pressure, then it decreases until the start of the relaxation phase.
During this relaxation phase, it increases suddenly to remain high throughout diastole.
During this phase, 70 to 80% of the myocardial flow of the LV is ensured.
In the RV, where the pressure is lower, coronary flow is ensured equally during systole and diastole; the contractility force of the RV is lower than that of the LV.
The heterogeneity of intramyocardial pressure distribution means that, particularly in the LV wall, the transmural distribution of CBF varies during the cardiac cycle.
During systole the subendocardial layers, directly subjected to intracavitary pressure, are poorly irrigated, while the subepicardial layers are correctly perfused.
During diastole, the subendocardial layers, which were hypoperfused during systole, are preferentially vasodilated and receive a larger fraction of the coronary flow.
The latter are therefore almost exclusively perfused during diastole while the subepicardial layers are perfused throughout the cardiac cycle.
Additionally, because mechanical work decreases from the endocardium to the epicardium, the subendocardial layers are those with the highest demand for O₂.
Then the subendocardial coronary flow is greater than the subepicardial flow and the subendocardial layers are the most sensitive to disturbances in myocardial perfusion.
In a subject at rest, the DSC is of the order of 80ml/min/100g of myocardium, which corresponds to 250ml/min for the entire organ (300g).
During vigorous exercise, DSC increases 4-5 times.
DSC is not continuous but pulsatile.

Under resting basal conditions, approximately 70% of O₂ from arterial blood is extracted as it passes through the coronary circulation. Thus the largest arteriovenous difference (DAVO₂) in the body, therefore the highest myocardial consumption of O₂ (MVO₂) 11ml/min/100g of myocardium (13% of the body's VO₂)
The myocardium has a high sampling power. But already at its maximum, this power can hardly rise.
It follows that the increase in oxygen supply, which any increase in myocardial activity requires, can only be achieved by an increase in CBF itself.
ΔP: perfusion pressure which is directly related to aortic pressure;
R: coronary vascular resistance; is the sum of vasomotion, blood viscosity and extrinsic resistance linked to systolic myocardial compression.
Coronary circulation is mainly regulated by the vasomotion of local arteries and arterioles.
The regulation of vasomotor function is mixed, metabolic and nervous.
Local metabolism is the main regulatory factor of vasomotor function. This mechanism works whether the heart is innervated or denervated.
As a result, CBF increases each time the force of contraction increases, whatever the cause. Conversely, CBF decreases when cardiac activity is less.
Variations in O₂ requirements are essentially the cause of this local regulation.
The close relationship between CBF and MVO₂ indicates that one or more of the metabolic products cause coronary vasodilation.
Factors likely to play this role include lack of O₂ and increased local concentrations of CO₂, H⁺, K⁺, lactate, prostaglandins, and adenosine.
The autonomic nervous system directly and indirectly controls coronary circulation.
1-Indirect effects opposed to direct effects are by far the most important:

Sympathetic stimulation responsible for the release of norepinephrine and adrenaline increases the frequency and force of cardiac contractions and thereby increases cardiac metabolism. Coronary vasodilation is caused by increased cardiac metabolism.

Parasympathetic stimulation decreases heart rate and cardiac contractility (decreased sympathetic discharge) and consequently, there is a decrease in cardiac metabolism responsible for coronary vasoconstriction.

At the level of the coronary arterioles, the density of β adrenergic receptors ensuring vasodilation is greater than the density of α adrenergic receptors responsible for vasoconstriction, which explains the weak contracting effect exerted by sympathetic stimulation and catecholamines on normal coronary microcirculation.
On the other hand, the vasodilator response following stimulation
β2-adrenergic is strong on the coronary microcirculation of humans and probably plays a determining role during exercise??

When systemic blood pressure falls, the overall effect of the reflex increase in noradrenergic discharge is the increase in CBF induced by metabolic changes in the myocardium at a time when cutaneous, renal, and splanchnic vessels are contracted.
In this way, the circulation of the heart, like that of the brain, is preserved even though it is compromised in other organs.

Coronary heart disease, responsible for mortality and known in the elderly, is becoming more and more common in the young. Knowing the physiology of coronary circulation means understanding the pathophysiology of coronary artery disease.
